dx: Necrotizing enterocolitis in a premature infant
case: A 12-day-old boy born at 29 weeks' gestation is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit because of feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools. He has been fed a cow's milk-based preterm formula since day 4 of life. Temperature is 36.0 °C (96.8 °F), pulse is 182/min, respirations are 64/min, and blood pressure is 50/30 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a distended, tender abdomen with erythema of the abdominal wall and absent bowel sounds. Gastric aspirates are bilious. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 82,000/mm3 (150,000 to 450,000) and an arterial pH of 7.24 (7.35 to 7.45). Diagnosis: necrotizing enterocolitis.

questions.stem: An abdominal radiograph is obtained. Which of the following radiographic findings is most likely?
options: Gas confined to a dilated stomach and duodenal bulb
Scattered calcifications along the peritoneal surfaces
Linear and bubbly gas within the bowel wall
Dilated loops with a bubbly mass in the right lower quadrant
approach: Name the core process: ischemic injury of immature mucosa followed by bacterial invasion.
Ask what invading bacteria produce inside damaged bowel: gas from fermentation.
Pick the finding that shows gas inside the bowel wall, called pneumatosis intestinalis.
questions.why: Necrotizing enterocolitis starts with mucosal injury in the immature bowel of a premature infant, aided by reduced blood flow, an immature barrier, and formula feeding. Bacteria cross the damaged mucosa and ferment luminal substrate, producing hydrogen gas that tracks into the submucosa and subserosa. On radiograph this gas appears as linear or bubbly lucencies in the bowel wall, called pneumatosis intestinalis, the hallmark finding. Gas can also enter the portal venous system, and free air means the bowel has perforated.
whyNot: This double bubble sign points to duodenal atresia, which presents within the first day of life with bilious vomiting and is linked to Down syndrome.
Peritoneal calcifications suggest meconium peritonitis from a bowel perforation that happened before birth.
Correct.
A bubbly right lower quadrant mass of thick meconium with dilated proximal loops suggests meconium ileus, an early sign of cystic fibrosis seen in the first days of life.

questions.stem: His mother was unable to provide breast milk. Human milk lowers the risk of this disease, partly because it contains secretory IgA directed against microbes from the mother's own intestine. In which of the following sites were the B cells that produce this milk IgA most likely first activated?
options: Peyer patches in the mother's ileum
Germinal centers in the mother's splenic white pulp
Mesenteric lymph nodes of the infant
Axillary lymph nodes that drain the mother's breast
approach: Note that the milk IgA targets the mother's gut microbes, so the B cells met those antigens in her gut.
Recall how gut antigens are sampled: M cells over Peyer patches pass them to underlying lymphoid follicles.
Link this to homing of IgA-committed B cells from the gut to other mucosal sites, including the lactating breast.
questions.why: M cells in the epithelium over Peyer patches take up luminal antigens and pass them to dendritic cells and B cells in the follicles below. Activated B cells switch to IgA and gain homing receptors that send them to mucosal tissues, including the lactating mammary gland, which is often called the enteromammary link. Plasma cells in the breast then secrete dimeric IgA that the polymeric Ig receptor carries into milk. The infant receives antibody aimed at exactly the microbes he is likely to meet from his mother, which helps protect the immature gut.
whyNot: Correct.
The spleen mounts systemic responses to blood-borne antigens, mainly IgM and IgG, and these B cells do not home to the breast.
A premature infant makes very little IgA of his own, and milk antibodies come from the mother.
Axillary nodes drain lymph from breast tissue, but the IgA plasma cells in milk-producing tissue are mostly gut-primed cells that homed there.

topics: Gut mucosal immunity and M cells

questions.stem: He undergoes resection of a necrotic segment of ileum. Microscopy shows mucosal necrosis and gas-filled cysts in the layer between the muscularis mucosae and the muscularis externa. Which of the following neural structures normally lies within this layer?
options: Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus
Prevertebral sympathetic ganglion cells
Parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies
Submucosal (Meissner) plexus
approach: Identify the layer: the tissue between the muscularis mucosae and the muscularis externa is the submucosa.
Recall which enteric plexus lies in the submucosa and which lies within the muscle coat.
Exclude neurons whose cell bodies lie outside the gut wall.
questions.why: The gut wall has four layers: mucosa (with its thin muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa or adventitia. The submucosa holds large vessels, lymphatics, and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, which mainly controls secretion and local blood flow. In necrotizing enterocolitis, gas cysts often collect in the submucosa and subserosa. If necrosis extends through the muscularis externa and serosa, the bowel perforates.
whyNot: The myenteric plexus lies between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and mainly controls motility.
Prevertebral ganglia, such as the celiac and superior mesenteric ganglia, sit outside the gut wall near the aorta. Only their postganglionic fibers reach the bowel.
Parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies lie in the brainstem (vagal nuclei) and sacral spinal cord (S2 to S4). Their fibers synapse on enteric neurons in the wall.
Correct.

questions.stem: Feeds are stopped for 10 days. In healthy people between meals, a cyclic wave of strong contractions sweeps undigested debris and bacteria from the stomach through the small intestine about every 90 minutes. Which of the following pairs this motor pattern with the hormone that triggers it?
options: Segmentation, triggered by cholecystokinin
Migrating motor complex, triggered by motilin
Receptive relaxation, triggered by vasoactive intestinal peptide
Mass movement, triggered by gastrin
approach: Note the timing (fasting) and the purpose (clearing debris and bacteria from the stomach and small bowel).
Name the pattern: the migrating motor complex.
Recall the hormone that starts its strongest phase: motilin from M cells of the upper small intestine.
questions.why: During fasting, the stomach and small intestine cycle through the migrating motor complex about every 90 to 120 minutes. Its phase III is a burst of strong peristaltic contractions that sweeps residue and bacteria toward the colon, acting as a housekeeper that limits bacterial overgrowth. Motilin, released from M cells of the duodenum and jejunum, rises in step with these bursts and triggers the gastric phase III. Eating interrupts the cycle and replaces it with the fed pattern.
whyNot: Segmentation mixes chyme with digestive juices in the fed state. Cholecystokinin is released by fat and protein after a meal.
Correct.
Receptive relaxation lets the proximal stomach accept a meal and is driven by vagal release of VIP and nitric oxide during swallowing.
Mass movements push colonic contents toward the rectum a few times a day, often after a meal as part of the gastrocolic reflex.

case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of epigastric discomfort and early satiety. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb). Physical examination shows mild epigastric tenderness and no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL (12 to 16). Upper endoscopy shows thickened, nodular mucosa in the gastric antrum with a shallow ulcer. Biopsy shows chronic active gastritis with curved bacilli in the surface mucus and a dense infiltrate of small, atypical lymphocytes that invade and destroy gastric glands (lymphoepithelial lesions). The lymphoma cells are CD20 positive. CT shows no disease beyond the stomach. Diagnosis: gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma with Helicobacter pylori infection.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of the biopsy shows that the lymphoma cells are CD5 negative and CD10 negative. Which of the following best describes the cell of origin of this tumor?
options: Mantle zone B cells with cyclin D1 overexpression
Marginal zone B cells of gastric lymphoid tissue
Germinal center B cells with BCL2 overexpression
Interstitial cells of Cajal with a KIT mutation
approach: Use the markers: CD20 positive means a B cell tumor; CD5 negative and CD10 negative exclude mantle cell and follicular lymphoma.
Recall that chronic H. pylori gastritis creates lymphoid follicles in a stomach that normally has none.
Match the tumor to the B cells in the marginal zone around these acquired follicles.
questions.why: The normal stomach has no organized lymphoid tissue. Chronic H. pylori infection induces lymphoid follicles, and MALT lymphoma arises from the marginal zone B cells around them, so it is an extranodal marginal zone B cell lymphoma. The cells are CD20 positive and typically CD5 and CD10 negative. Lymphoepithelial lesions, where tumor cells invade and destroy glands, are characteristic.
whyNot: Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5 positive and carries t(11;14), which overexpresses cyclin D1.
Correct.
Follicular lymphoma comes from germinal center B cells, is CD10 positive, and carries t(14;18), which overexpresses BCL2.
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor arises from interstitial cells of Cajal, is CD117 (KIT) positive, and is a spindle cell tumor without CD20.

questions.stem: She receives a proton pump inhibitor, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin. Six months later, a urea breath test is negative and repeat biopsies show regression of the lymphoma. Which of the following best explains this response?
options: Clarithromycin is directly cytotoxic to the lymphoma cells
Lower gastric acid removes a growth signal from the B cells
Antibodies against the organism lyse tumor cells by complement
Growth depends on help from H. pylori-specific T cells
approach: Recall that early MALT lymphoma is still driven by the chronic antigen that started it.
Identify the source of the growth signal: CD4 T cells that recognize H. pylori antigens and help the B cells.
Predict that removing the antigen removes T cell help, so the tumor shrinks.
questions.why: In early gastric MALT lymphoma, the tumor B cells still depend on stimulation from H. pylori-specific CD4 T cells, which supply CD40 ligand and cytokines. When the infection is cured, the antigen is gone, T cell help stops, and many tumors regress. Tumors that carry t(11;18), which joins API2 and MALT1, activate NF-kB on their own and usually do not respond to eradication alone.
whyNot: Clarithromycin is given to kill H. pylori. It has no meaningful direct effect on lymphoma cells.
Acid suppression helps the antibiotics work and heals the ulcer, but acid does not drive B cell growth.
Antibodies to H. pylori bind the bacteria. The tumor B cells do not display H. pylori antigens for these antibodies to target.
Correct.

topics: T cell help for B cells

questions.stem: H. pylori infection also raises her risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following sequences most likely precedes the H. pylori-associated type of this cancer?
options: Atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia
Germline CDH1 loss, then signet ring cells infiltrating singly
Foveolar hyperplasia with giant rugal folds and protein loss
Reflux esophagitis, then columnar metaplasia at the cardia
approach: Recall the two Lauren types of gastric adenocarcinoma: intestinal and diffuse.
Link chronic H. pylori gastritis to the intestinal type.
Trace the stepwise path of mucosal injury that leads to gland-forming cancer.
questions.why: Intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma follows years of chronic injury. H. pylori gastritis, sometimes with dietary nitrosamines, causes atrophy of the glands, then intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells, then dysplasia, and finally an invasive carcinoma that forms glands. The diffuse type has a weaker link to environmental injury and grows as single signet ring cells that thicken the wall.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) causes diffuse-type carcinoma, with signet ring cells and a rigid linitis plastica stomach. Germline CDH1 mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.
Giant rugal folds with protein loss and foveolar hyperplasia describe Menetrier disease, a hypertrophic gastropathy that is not the usual path to H. pylori-related cancer.
Reflux injury and columnar metaplasia lead to Barrett esophagus and adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus and gastroesophageal junction. H. pylori is not a risk factor for these.

questions.stem: Her gastritis is most severe in the antrum. Another patient has autoimmune gastritis that destroys the mucosa of the gastric body and fundus but spares the antrum. Which of the following secretion changes is most likely in that patient?
options: Low serum gastrin, high acid, normal intrinsic factor
Low pepsinogen, normal acid, low serum gastrin
Low acid and intrinsic factor, high serum gastrin
Low serum gastrin and acid, normal intrinsic factor
approach: Map the cells: body and fundus glands contain parietal cells (HCl and intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen); G cells live in the antrum.
Predict loss of acid and intrinsic factor when body and fundus mucosa is destroyed.
Apply feedback: with no acid, antral D cells release less somatostatin, so the spared G cells oversecrete gastrin.
questions.why: Autoimmune gastritis targets parietal cells and intrinsic factor in the body and fundus. Losing parietal cells removes HCl and intrinsic factor, which leads to achlorhydria and, over time, vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia). Chief cells are also lost, so pepsinogen I falls. The antrum is spared, and without acid to trigger somatostatin, G cells release large amounts of gastrin. In her antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis, by contrast, acid output is often normal or high.
whyNot: High acid with low gastrin does not fit loss of parietal cells. With no parietal cells, acid falls.
Pepsinogen does fall, but parietal cells are destroyed along with chief cells, so acid cannot stay normal, and gastrin rises.
Correct.
Acid falls, but gastrin rises because acid feedback is lost, and intrinsic factor falls with the parietal cells.

dx: Small intestinal carcinoid tumor with carcinoid syndrome
case: A 59-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of episodes of facial flushing and watery diarrhea several times daily. He also has intermittent wheezing. Physical examination shows a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration, and a firm, nodular, enlarged liver. A 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) level is 96 mg (2 to 8). CT shows a 2-cm mass in the distal ileum, enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, and multiple liver masses. Biopsy of a liver mass shows nests of uniform cells that stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin. Diagnosis: metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor of the ileum with carcinoid syndrome.

questions.stem: Echocardiography shows thickened, fixed tricuspid and pulmonic valve leaflets, while the mitral and aortic valves are normal. Which of the following best explains why the left-sided valves are spared?
options: Higher left-sided pressures wash away fibrous plaques
Left-sided endocardium lacks serotonin receptors
Hepatic metastases release serotonin into the bile
Pulmonary monoamine oxidase inactivates serotonin
approach: Trace tumor products from liver metastases: hepatic veins, inferior vena cava, right heart.
Ask what happens to serotonin as blood passes through the lungs.
Conclude that only right-sided valves see high serotonin levels.
questions.why: Liver metastases release serotonin and other vasoactive products directly into the hepatic veins, so they reach the right heart without first-pass clearance. Serotonin stimulates fibroblasts to lay down plaque-like fibrous tissue on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves, causing regurgitation and stenosis. The lungs contain monoamine oxidase and clear much of the serotonin before blood reaches the left heart, so the mitral and aortic valves are usually spared. Left-sided lesions appear with a right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale, or with a bronchial carcinoid.
whyNot: Valve plaques reflect exposure to tumor products. Pressure differences do not remove them.
Both sides of the heart have similar tissue. The difference is how much serotonin each side receives.
Serotonin from liver metastases enters hepatic venous blood. Biliary release would not explain the valve pattern.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before the tumor spread to the liver, he had no flushing, although the ileal tumor was already secreting serotonin. Which of the following venous pathways carried this serotonin to the site where it was inactivated?
options: Ileal veins, inferior mesenteric vein, left renal vein, inferior vena cava
Ileal veins, superior mesenteric vein, portal vein, sinusoids
Ileal veins, right gonadal vein, inferior vena cava
Ileal veins, splenic vein, hepatic veins, then portal vein
approach: Identify that ileal venous blood drains to the liver before reaching the systemic circulation.
Trace the vessels: superior mesenteric vein, joining the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
Recall that hepatocytes inactivate serotonin as portal blood passes through the sinusoids.
questions.why: Veins of the ileum drain into the superior mesenteric vein. Behind the neck of the pancreas the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein, which enters the liver and branches into sinusoids. Hepatocytes break down serotonin with monoamine oxidase, so little reaches the central veins, hepatic veins, and inferior vena cava. Once tumor grows in the liver, its products enter the hepatic veins directly and bypass this first-pass clearance, which is why the syndrome usually appears after liver metastasis.
whyNot: The inferior mesenteric vein drains the descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum and usually joins the splenic vein. It does not drain to the left renal vein, and the ileum does not drain into it.
Correct.
The gonadal veins drain the testes or ovaries. The gut drains through the portal system.
The ileum does not drain to the splenic vein, and blood flows from the portal vein into the liver and out through the hepatic veins, in that order.

questions.stem: He also develops a scaly, hyperpigmented rash on the sun-exposed skin of his neck and forearms, a red, swollen tongue, and difficulty concentrating. Deficiency of which of the following cofactors best explains these new findings?
options: Thiamine pyrophosphate
Biotin
NAD+ and NADP+
Ascorbate
approach: Recognize pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, glossitis, and mental changes.
Recall that tryptophan is a precursor of both serotonin and niacin.
Link niacin to its cofactor forms, NAD+ and NADP+.
questions.why: Carcinoid tumors can divert a large share of dietary tryptophan into serotonin. Less tryptophan is left to make niacin, so niacin and its cofactors NAD+ and NADP+ fall. Many dehydrogenases in energy metabolism need these electron carriers, and tissues with high turnover, such as skin, gut, and brain, show the deficiency first. The result is pellagra: dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, glossitis, and confusion or dementia.
whyNot: Thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy and beriberi (neuropathy or heart failure), without a photosensitive rash.
Biotin deficiency, seen with heavy raw egg white intake, causes a scaly rash around the face, hair loss, and lethargy, without a sun-exposed pattern.
Correct.
Ascorbate deficiency causes scurvy, with bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and poor wound healing from impaired collagen hydroxylation.

questions.stem: He is kept fasting for 48 hours, and the large-volume watery diarrhea continues. Stool sodium is 95 mEq/L, stool potassium is 45 mEq/L, and measured stool osmolality is 290 mOsm/kg. Which of the following best classifies his diarrhea?
options: Secretory, with a stool osmotic gap of about 10 mOsm/kg
Osmotic, with a stool osmotic gap of about 10 mOsm/kg
Secretory, with a stool osmotic gap of about 150 mOsm/kg
Osmotic, with a stool osmotic gap of about 150 mOsm/kg
approach: Calculate the gap: 290 minus 2 times (95 plus 45) equals 290 minus 280, or about 10 mOsm/kg.
Interpret it: a gap below about 50 means electrolytes account for the stool water, which fits secretory diarrhea.
Confirm with fasting: secretory diarrhea continues without food, while osmotic diarrhea stops.
questions.why: The stool osmotic gap is 290 minus 2 times the sum of stool sodium and potassium. Here it is about 10 mOsm/kg. A small gap, below about 50, means the water in stool is held by secreted electrolytes, which is secretory diarrhea. A large gap, above about 100, means an unmeasured solute such as unabsorbed lactose is holding water, which is osmotic diarrhea. Serotonin and other tumor products drive intestinal secretion and speed motility, so his diarrhea persists during fasting.
whyNot: Correct.
The gap is small, which points away from an unabsorbed solute. Osmotic diarrhea also stops with fasting.
His values give a gap of about 10, and a gap of 150 would mean an unmeasured solute was present.
A gap of 150 with diarrhea that stops on fasting would fit osmotic diarrhea, such as lactose intolerance. His numbers do not give this gap, and his diarrhea continued.

dx: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with a pancreatic gastrinoma
case: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of burning epigastric pain, watery diarrhea, and loose, greasy stools. She has had two kidney stones, and her brother had a parathyroid adenoma removed. Upper endoscopy shows prominent, thickened gastric folds and multiple ulcers, including ulcers in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum. Laboratory studies show a serum calcium of 11.4 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.5) and a fasting serum gastrin of 1,250 pg/mL (less than 100), with a gastric pH of 1.5. CT shows a 2-cm mass in the head of the pancreas. Genetic testing shows a germline MEN1 mutation. Diagnosis: multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with a pancreatic gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).

questions.stem: Before the CT, a secretin stimulation test was done to confirm the cause of her hypergastrinemia. Which of the following results is most likely?
options: Serum gastrin rises sharply
Serum gastrin falls by half
Serum gastrin does not change
Serum gastrin falls below 100 pg/mL
approach: Recall that secretin normally inhibits gastrin release from antral G cells.
Recall that gastrinoma cells respond to secretin in the opposite way.
Predict a paradoxical rise in gastrin, which confirms a gastrinoma.
questions.why: In healthy people, secretin suppresses gastrin release from G cells. Gastrinoma cells express secretin receptors that stimulate gastrin release, so intravenous secretin causes a sharp, paradoxical rise in serum gastrin, commonly defined as an increase of 120 pg/mL or more. Her low gastric pH with very high gastrin already argues against causes of high gastrin with low acid, such as atrophic gastritis or proton pump inhibitor use, and the secretin test confirms an autonomous tumor.
whyNot: Correct.

Secretin does not raise gastrin release from normal G cells, so a fall or no change is expected when high gastrin comes from normal G cells, as in atrophic gastritis or proton pump inhibitor use. A gastrinoma responds with a rise.
An unchanged level would not support a gastrinoma. Tumor cells respond to secretin with a rise.
Normalization of gastrin would mean the gastrin source is suppressible normal tissue, which does not fit a tumor.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, a meal that delivers acid and fat into the duodenum triggers hormones that slow gastric emptying, neutralize the acid, and contract the gallbladder. Which of the following hormone and source cell pairs are released in response?
options: Gastrin from G cells and motilin from M cells
Secretin from I cells and CCK from S cells
Secretin from S cells and CCK from I cells
Motilin from M cells and GIP from K cells
approach: Acid in the duodenum is the main stimulus for secretin, from S cells.
Fat and protein in the duodenum release cholecystokinin (CCK), from I cells.
Check the actions: secretin brings bicarbonate; CCK contracts the gallbladder, releases pancreatic enzymes, and slows gastric emptying.
questions.why: Acid entering the duodenum releases secretin from S cells, which drives pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion to neutralize the acid. Fatty acids and amino acids release cholecystokinin from I cells, which contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, and slows gastric emptying. Fat and glucose also release GIP from K cells, which boosts insulin release.
whyNot: Gastrin rises during the gastric phase in response to peptides and vagal input, and acid in the gut suppresses it. Motilin acts in the fasting state.
These hormones are correct, but their source cells are reversed. S cells make secretin and I cells make CCK.
Correct.
GIP does rise after fat, but motilin is a fasting hormone that drives the migrating motor complex and falls after a meal.

questions.stem: The thickened gastric folds seen at endoscopy reflect the trophic effect of gastrin on the mucosa of the gastric body. Which of the following best describes the hyperplastic cell type responsible for her high acid output?
options: Chief cells, which also secrete gastric lipase
Parietal cells, which also secrete intrinsic factor
Surface mucous cells, which also secrete bicarbonate
Antral G cells, which also secrete somatostatin
approach: Identify the acid-secreting cell of the gastric body glands.
Recall the other product of that same cell.
Link gastrin's growth effect to an expanded parietal cell mass and thick rugal folds.
questions.why: Gastrin acts on parietal cells directly and through histamine from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. Over time it also acts as a growth factor, expanding the parietal cell and ECL cell mass and thickening the folds of the body and fundus. Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor, which binds vitamin B12 for absorption in the ileum. A larger parietal cell mass explains her very high acid output and her low gastric pH.
whyNot: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase. They do not secrete acid.
Correct.
Surface mucous cells secrete mucus and bicarbonate that protect the mucosa. They do not secrete acid.
Antral G cells secrete gastrin, while somatostatin comes from D cells. Her gastrin comes from the tumor, and G cells do not secrete acid.

questions.stem: Her stools contain excess fat even though her pancreas secretes normal amounts of digestive enzymes. Which of the following best explains her steatorrhea?
options: Gastrin directly inhibits pancreatic lipase release
Bile salt synthesis by hepatocytes is suppressed
Excess CCK release depletes bile in the gallbladder
Low duodenal pH inactivates pancreatic lipase
approach: Recall that pancreatic lipase, with colipase and bile salts, digests triglycerides in the duodenum at a near-neutral pH.
Note that a gastrinoma delivers far more acid than pancreatic bicarbonate can neutralize.
Predict that acid inactivates lipase and impairs micelle formation, so fat goes unabsorbed.
questions.why: Fat digestion depends on pancreatic lipase and colipase acting at the surface of fat droplets that bile salts have emulsified. These steps work at a near-neutral pH, which pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate normally provide. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome the acid load overwhelms this buffering, so lipase is inactivated and bile acids precipitate and cannot form micelles. Acid injury to the small bowel mucosa adds to the malabsorption, and the large fluid load adds to the diarrhea.
whyNot: Gastrin does not block lipase release. Her pancreas releases normal amounts of enzyme.
Bile salt synthesis is normal. The problem is that bile acids precipitate in an acid duodenum.
CCK is released normally by fat. Gallbladder contraction delivers bile, and bile is not depleted in this condition.
Correct.

dx: Oral leukoplakia in a smoker with chronic periodontitis
case: A 61-year-old man comes to the dentist because of a painless white patch on his tongue that he noticed 3 months ago. He has smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinks 4 to 5 beers daily. Examination shows a 1.5-cm white, well-demarcated plaque on the right lateral border of the anterior two thirds of the tongue that does not rub off with gauze. His gingiva is red and swollen and bleeds on probing, with deep periodontal pockets and several loose molars. Dental radiographs show loss of alveolar bone around the molars. Diagnosis: oral leukoplakia and chronic periodontitis.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the tongue plaque is performed. Which of the following histologic findings would most strongly indicate a risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma?
options: Thickened surface keratin with no atypia
Budding yeast and pseudohyphae within keratin
Epithelial dysplasia with atypical mitoses
Ballooned superficial cells with EBV inclusions
approach: Recognize leukoplakia as a clinical term for a white plaque that cannot be scraped off and has no other cause.
Recall that its cancer risk depends on what the biopsy shows.
Pick the finding that marks a precancerous change in the squamous epithelium.
questions.why: Leukoplakia is a clinical description, and biopsy shows a range from simple hyperkeratosis to dysplasia to carcinoma. Dysplasia, with atypical nuclei, loss of normal maturation, and abnormal mitoses above the basal layer, is a precursor of invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Tobacco and alcohol act together as the main risks for oral squamous cell carcinoma, and lesions on the lateral tongue and floor of the mouth carry the highest risk.
whyNot: Hyperkeratosis without atypia is the most common biopsy result and carries a low risk of cancer.
Yeast and pseudohyphae mean candidiasis, whose white plaques scrape off. Candida can also colonize leukoplakia, but it is not the marker of cancer risk.
Correct.
Ballooned cells with EBV point to oral hairy leukoplakia, a benign lesion of the lateral tongue in immunosuppressed patients such as those with HIV.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms and mechanisms best explains the destruction of tooth-supporting tissue in his gum disease?
options: Streptococcus mutans, by fermenting sucrose to lactic acid
Actinomyces israelii, by forming sulfur granules in sinus tracts
Candida albicans, by invading the epithelium with hyphae
Porphyromonas gingivalis, through inflammatory bone resorption
approach: Separate the two plaque diseases: caries destroys tooth mineral, and periodontitis destroys the ligament and bone that hold the tooth.
Recall the key anaerobe of subgingival plaque in periodontitis.
Link its products to host inflammation and osteoclast activation.
questions.why: Plaque at the gum line first causes gingivitis, which is reversible with good oral hygiene. When the subgingival biofilm shifts toward gram-negative anaerobes such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, the inflammation deepens. Bacterial proteases (gingipains) and lipopolysaccharide drive a host response with cytokines and RANKL that activates osteoclasts. The periodontal ligament and alveolar bone are lost, pockets deepen, and teeth loosen.
whyNot: Streptococcus mutans makes acid from sucrose that dissolves enamel and causes dental caries, which can lead to a tooth abscess. It does not destroy the periodontal ligament and bone.
Actinomyces israelii causes cervicofacial actinomycosis, a slowly spreading infection with draining sinus tracts and sulfur granules, often after dental work.
Candida causes oral thrush with white plaques that scrape off. It is not the driver of periodontal bone loss.
Correct.

questions.stem: The lesion is excised. Afterward, he has loss of both general sensation and taste over the right anterior two thirds of the tongue, and tongue protrusion is normal. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains these deficits?
options: Lingual nerve
Chorda tympani in the middle ear
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
approach: Map the anterior two thirds: general sensation by the lingual nerve (V3), taste by chorda tympani fibers (VII).
Recall that chorda tympani fibers join the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa and run with it to the tongue.
Pick the one nerve that carries both modalities at the site of surgery.
questions.why: General sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue travels in the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3). Taste from the same area travels in the chorda tympani (facial nerve), whose fibers join the lingual nerve and run with it along the side of the tongue. Injury to the lingual nerve near the tongue therefore removes both touch and taste. Motor function is intact because the hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles.
whyNot: Correct.
A chorda tympani lesion in the middle ear removes taste from the anterior two thirds and reduces submandibular and sublingual secretion, but general sensation is spared.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries both taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue.
The hypoglossal nerve is motor. A lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the injured side on protrusion, without sensory loss.

questions.stem: His tobacco and alcohol use also increase his risk of squamous cell carcinoma at another site in the digestive tract that is lined by the same type of epithelium as the lateral tongue. Which of the following sites has this epithelium?
options: Gastric cardia
Middle third of the esophagus
Duodenal bulb
Anal canal above the pectinate line
approach: Identify the lining of the lateral tongue: nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Find the gut segment with the same lining.
Link shared epithelium and shared carcinogen exposure to shared squamous cell carcinoma risk.
questions.why: The lateral tongue, floor of mouth, and esophagus are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Tobacco smoke and alcohol bathe this whole upper aerodigestive lining, so a patient with oral squamous lesions is also at higher risk for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, which most often arises in the middle third. Below the gastroesophageal junction the lining changes to simple columnar epithelium, where adenocarcinomas arise instead.
whyNot: The gastric cardia is lined by simple columnar epithelium. Cancers here are adenocarcinomas.
Correct.
The duodenum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with villi and goblet cells.
Above the pectinate line the anal canal has columnar epithelium. Stratified squamous epithelium lies below the line.

case: A 72-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 4 days of profuse watery diarrhea, about 10 stools daily, with lower abdominal cramps. Eight days ago she finished a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender. Leukocyte count is 19,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). A stool PCR assay is positive for the toxin B gene. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows multiple raised yellow-white plaques on erythematous colonic mucosa. Diagnosis: Clostridioides difficile pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.stem: A biopsy of one of the plaques is taken. Which of the following best describes the composition of the plaques?
options: Necrotic squamous cells with budding yeast
Fibrin, mucin, and neutrophils from damaged crypts
A thick collagen band under intact surface epithelium
Granulomas with central caseous necrosis
approach: Connect the clinical setting (recent clindamycin, toxin B gene) to toxin-mediated colitis.
Recall how toxin damage to crypts produces the yellow-white plaques.
Pick the exudate that erupts from injured crypts.
questions.why: Antibiotics such as clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins disrupt the normal colonic flora and let C. difficile overgrow. Its toxins A and B injure the surface epithelium and crypts, which release a mushroom-shaped exudate of fibrin, mucin, neutrophils, and cell debris. These pseudomembranes form the yellow-white plaques seen at endoscopy. Severe disease can progress to toxic megacolon and perforation.
whyNot: Necrotic squamous cells with yeast describe Candida plaques, which form on squamous mucosa such as the mouth and esophagus.
Correct.
A thick subepithelial collagen band describes collagenous colitis, a cause of chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colon.
Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis, which can involve the ileocecal region and does not form surface pseudomembranes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the toxins of this organism injure colonic epithelial cells?
options: Glucosylation of Rho GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton
ADP-ribosylation of the Gs alpha subunit, raising cyclic AMP in enterocytes
Cleavage of 28S ribosomal RNA, halting protein synthesis
Cross-linking MHC class II and T cell receptors as a superantigen
approach: Recall that C. difficile toxins A and B are glucosyltransferases.
Identify their targets, the Rho family GTPases that control the actin cytoskeleton.
Predict cell rounding, loss of tight junctions, cell death, and inflammation.
questions.why: Toxins A and B enter colonocytes and add glucose to Rho, Rac, and Cdc42, the small GTPases that organize actin. The actin cytoskeleton collapses, tight junctions open, and cells round up and die. The damage triggers strong neutrophil recruitment, fluid loss, and pseudomembranes. Toxin B is the more potent cytotoxin, and stool PCR targets the toxin B gene because nearly all disease-causing strains carry it, including strains that lack toxin A.
whyNot: Correct.
Cholera toxin and the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli ADP-ribosylate Gs, raise cAMP, and open CFTR, causing large-volume watery diarrhea without cell death.
Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxins of EHEC cleave 28S rRNA in the 60S subunit and stop protein synthesis.
Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxins act as superantigens. Preformed toxin in food causes vomiting within a few hours.

topics: C. difficile toxins A and B

questions.stem: On the third day her abdominal distension worsens. An abdominal radiograph shows a markedly dilated transverse colon that has lost its normal haustral markings. Which of the following structures normally produces the haustra?
options: Plicae circulares
Omental appendices
Transverse rectal folds
Taeniae coli
approach: Recognize the radiograph: a dilated colon without haustra in severe colitis suggests toxic megacolon.
Recall what haustra are: sacculations of the colon wall seen only in the large intestine.
Pick the colon feature that gathers the wall into these sacs: the taeniae coli.
questions.why: In the colon, the outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three bands, the taeniae coli. The taeniae are shorter than the colon wall, so the wall bunches into sacs between them, called haustra. Haustra, taeniae coli, and omental appendices together mark large intestine on gross inspection and imaging. In toxic megacolon, inflammation spreads into the muscle layer, muscle tone is lost, and the dilated colon loses its haustral pattern, which raises the risk of perforation.
whyNot: Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds of mucosa and submucosa in the small intestine. On radiograph they cross the full width of the bowel, unlike haustral markings.
Omental appendices are small fat-filled pouches of peritoneum on the outer colon surface. They help identify the colon but do not form the haustra.
Transverse rectal folds are shelves of mucosa, submucosa, and circular muscle inside the rectum, which has no haustra.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of stool findings best fits the type of diarrhea she has?
options: No leukocytes; gap above 100 mOsm/kg; stops with fasting
No leukocytes; gap below 50 mOsm/kg; continues with fasting
Leukocytes and lactoferrin present; continues with fasting
No leukocytes; high fecal fat; stops with fasting
approach: Classify her illness: toxins destroy the mucosa and recruit neutrophils, which is inflammatory diarrhea.
Recall the stool marker of inflammation: leukocytes, or lactoferrin and calprotectin released by neutrophils.
Recall that inflammatory diarrhea does not depend on eating, so it continues with fasting.
questions.why: Diarrhea is grouped as secretory, osmotic, or inflammatory. In inflammatory diarrhea, damaged mucosa leaks fluid, protein, and cells, and neutrophils enter the lumen, so stool contains leukocytes and neutrophil proteins such as lactoferrin and calprotectin. Fever and leukocytosis are common. Because the problem is mucosal injury, the diarrhea continues during fasting.
whyNot: A large osmotic gap that resolves with fasting describes osmotic diarrhea, such as lactose intolerance or laxative use.
A small gap without leukocytes that continues with fasting describes pure secretory diarrhea, such as cholera.
Correct.
High fecal fat that stops with fasting suggests fat malabsorption, such as pancreatic insufficiency.

case: A 27-year-old man who works at a child care center comes to the physician because of 2 days of fever, crampy lower abdominal pain, and frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus. He has painful straining to pass stool. Several children at the center have had a similar illness this week. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. The lower abdomen is tender. Stool microscopy shows many neutrophils and erythrocytes. Stool culture grows Shigella sonnei. Diagnosis: Shigella dysentery (shigellosis).

questions.stem: Three weeks after the diarrhea resolves, he develops a painful, swollen right knee, bilateral conjunctivitis, and dysuria. Synovial fluid culture is sterile. Which of the following host factors most increases the risk of this complication?
options: HLA-DR3
HLA-DR4
HLA-DQ2
HLA-B27
approach: Recognize reactive arthritis: sterile arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis weeks after an enteric or genital infection.
Recall the enteric triggers: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, and Yersinia.
Link reactive arthritis to its MHC class I association.
questions.why: Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that follows infection elsewhere, most often enteric infection with Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Yersinia, or genital infection with Chlamydia. It typically affects large joints of the legs and may come with conjunctivitis and urethritis. Many patients carry HLA-B27, the same allele linked to ankylosing spondylitis and the other seronegative spondyloarthropathies.
whyNot: HLA-DR3 is linked to type 1 diabetes, Graves disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.
HLA-DQ2 (with DQ8) is linked to celiac disease.
Correct.

questions.stem: The infection spread quickly among the children by person-to-person contact without a common food source. Which of the following features of the organism best explains this pattern?
options: A reservoir in the intestines of poultry flocks
Flagellar motility toward the mucosal surface
Infection with as few as 10 to 100 organisms
A reservoir in reptiles such as pet turtles
approach: Note the pattern: spread by direct contact among young children, with no food vehicle.
Recall which enteric pathogen needs only a tiny inoculum.
Link low infectious dose to easy fecal-oral spread on hands and surfaces.
questions.why: Shigella resists gastric acid well, so as few as 10 to 100 organisms can cause disease. A tiny inoculum on hands or toys is enough, which makes person-to-person spread easy in child care centers and other crowded settings. Humans are its only reservoir. Shigella is nonmotile and does not produce H2S, which helps separate it from Salmonella in the laboratory.
whyNot: A poultry reservoir fits Campylobacter jejuni and Salmonella, which usually spread through undercooked chicken.
Shigella is nonmotile. Salmonella and Campylobacter are motile.
Correct.
Reptiles, such as pet turtles, are a reservoir for nontyphoidal Salmonella, which needs a much larger dose to cause disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains why his stools are frequent and small in volume and contain blood, mucus, and neutrophils, unlike the large-volume stools of cholera?
options: Cyclic AMP-driven chloride secretion through CFTR
Invasion and destruction of the colonic mucosa
Unabsorbed solute holding water in the lumen
Serotonin-driven increase in intestinal motility
approach: Identify the clues to inflammatory diarrhea: blood, mucus, neutrophils, fever, tenesmus.
Recall that Shigella enters through M cells and spreads cell to cell in the colonic epithelium.
Link an inflamed, irritable rectosigmoid colon to frequent small stools.
questions.why: Shigella invades the colonic epithelium, spreads from cell to cell, and kills the cells, which produces ulcers and intense neutrophil infiltration. The damaged mucosa leaks blood, mucus, and inflammatory cells into the lumen. An inflamed rectum and sigmoid colon hold little stool and cause urgency and tenesmus, so stools are frequent and small. Cholera, by contrast, leaves the mucosa intact and makes the small intestine secrete liters of fluid.
whyNot: Cholera toxin raises cAMP and opens CFTR, causing large-volume, watery stools without blood or neutrophils.
Correct.
Unabsorbed solute, such as lactose, causes osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting and has no blood or neutrophils.
Serotonin drives secretion and speeds transit in carcinoid syndrome, causing watery diarrhea without mucosal destruction.

questions.stem: His roommate returns from travel with prolonged fever and is found to have typhoid fever with ulcers in the terminal ileum. Which of the following histologic features would identify a biopsy as ileum rather than jejunum or duodenum?
options: Large lymphoid aggregates in the submucosa
Mucous glands deep in the submucosa
Tall, closely spaced circular folds with villi
Crypts rich in goblet cells and no villi
approach: Recall the identifying feature of each small bowel segment.
Match the ileum to Peyer patches, the large lymphoid aggregates that extend into the submucosa.
Link Salmonella Typhi to invasion through M cells over Peyer patches, which explains the ileal ulcers.
questions.why: Peyer patches are clusters of lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa of the ileum, covered by M cells that sample luminal antigens. Salmonella Typhi enters through these M cells, multiplies in macrophages, and spreads through the blood. Inflammation and necrosis of the Peyer patches produce ulcers in the terminal ileum, which can bleed or perforate.
whyNot: Correct.
Submucosal mucous glands are Brunner glands, which identify the duodenum.
Tall, closely spaced plicae circulares are the hallmark of the jejunum.
Goblet cell-rich crypts without villi identify the colon.

dx: Candida esophagitis and oral thrush in advanced HIV infection
case: A 38-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of painful swallowing and a sore mouth. He has lost 6 kg (13.2 lb). Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa and palate that scrape off and leave a red, bleeding base. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 62/mm3 (500 to 1,500). Upper endoscopy shows numerous adherent white plaques along the length of the esophagus. Diagnosis: Candida esophagitis and oral thrush in advanced HIV infection.

questions.stem: Biopsy specimens are taken from the esophageal plaques. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Budding yeast and pseudohyphae in a fibrinous exudate
Multinucleated squamous cells with intranuclear inclusions at ulcer edges
Enlarged endothelial cells with inclusions at the base of linear ulcers
More than 15 eosinophils per high-power field in the epithelium
approach: Match the endoscopic pattern: white plaques point to Candida, punched-out ulcers to HSV, and long linear ulcers to CMV.
Recall the tissue form of Candida albicans.
Pick yeast with pseudohyphae in the plaque material.
questions.why: Candida albicans grows in tissue as budding yeast with pseudohyphae, best shown with PAS or silver stains. In the esophagus it forms white plaques of fungus, fibrin, and debris that stick to the squamous lining. In patients with HIV and low CD4 counts, Candida is the most common cause of infectious esophagitis, and esophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining illness.
whyNot: Correct.
Multinucleated squamous cells with ground-glass intranuclear inclusions at the edges of small, punched-out ulcers describe HSV esophagitis.
Inclusions in endothelial and stromal cells at the base of long, shallow linear ulcers describe CMV esophagitis.
Many intraepithelial eosinophils describe eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic disorder with rings and furrows.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions also predisposes to oral infection by this organism by impairing local mucosal defenses?
options: Splenectomy after abdominal trauma
Inhaled corticosteroid use without rinsing
Deficiency of terminal complement components
Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor
approach: Recall that mucosal control of Candida depends on T cells (especially Th17 cells) and a balanced oral flora.
Look for a condition that suppresses local immunity in the mouth.
Exclude defects that mainly raise risk from encapsulated bacteria, Neisseria, or swelling.
questions.why: Oral thrush is overgrowth of Candida albicans, which normally lives in the mouth in small numbers. It appears when local defenses or the competing flora fail: in young infants, with inhaled corticosteroids that deposit in the mouth, after broad-spectrum antibiotics, in diabetes, in denture wearers, and in HIV with falling CD4 counts. Steroid from an inhaler suppresses local immunity, which is why patients are told to rinse after each use.
whyNot: Splenectomy raises the risk of sepsis from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Correct.
Terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency raises the risk of recurrent Neisseria infections.
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, with recurrent swelling and no infection risk.

questions.stem: At endoscopy, the paler esophageal lining meets the redder gastric lining at an irregular line near the gastroesophageal junction. Which of the following epithelial transitions normally occurs at this line?
options: Keratinized stratified squamous to simple cuboidal
Pseudostratified columnar to simple columnar
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous to goblet cell-rich columnar
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous to simple columnar
approach: Recall the normal esophageal lining: nonkeratinized stratified squamous.
Recall the normal gastric lining: simple columnar mucus-secreting cells.
Recognize that goblet cells above this line would be abnormal intestinal metaplasia.
questions.why: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which resists abrasion from swallowed food. At the squamocolumnar junction, or Z line, it changes abruptly to the simple columnar, mucus-secreting epithelium of the stomach. With chronic acid reflux, columnar epithelium with goblet cells can replace the distal esophageal squamous lining. This intestinal metaplasia is Barrett esophagus, the precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma.
whyNot: The esophagus is nonkeratinized in humans, and the stomach is lined by columnar cells.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the trachea and bronchi.
Columnar epithelium with goblet cells at or above the junction is Barrett metaplasia, an abnormal change caused by chronic reflux.
Correct.

questions.stem: During swallowing, the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes as the peristaltic wave approaches it. Which of the following mediates this relaxation?
options: Acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors
Norepinephrine released from postganglionic sympathetic fibers
Nitric oxide and VIP from vagal inhibitory pathways
Gastrin released from antral G cells
approach: Recall that swallowing is coordinated by the swallowing center in the medulla.
Recall that vagal fibers synapse on enteric inhibitory neurons at the sphincter.
Identify their transmitters: nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide.
questions.why: Swallowing begins with a voluntary oral phase, then a reflex pharyngeal phase and esophageal phase coordinated by the medulla through the vagus nerves. As peristalsis starts, vagal fibers activate inhibitory neurons of the myenteric plexus at the lower esophageal sphincter. These neurons release nitric oxide and VIP, which relax the sphincter smooth muscle so the bolus can enter the stomach. Loss of these inhibitory neurons causes achalasia.
whyNot: Acetylcholine from excitatory vagal pathways contracts esophageal smooth muscle and maintains sphincter tone.
Sympathetic input does not drive the swallow-induced relaxation of the sphincter.
Correct.
Gastrin does not mediate the swallow-induced relaxation of the sphincter.

dx: Norovirus gastroenteritis in a cruise ship outbreak
case: A 67-year-old woman comes to the ship's physician during a cruise because of sudden nausea, repeated vomiting, and watery, nonbloody diarrhea that began 14 hours ago. More than 100 other passengers and crew members have had similar symptoms over the past 3 days. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Mucous membranes are dry. Serum sodium is 136 mEq/L (135 to 145), and serum creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Reverse transcription PCR of stool is positive for norovirus. Diagnosis: norovirus gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: On the same voyage, a crew member eats fried rice that was cooked the day before, left at room temperature, and then reheated. Two hours later he develops nausea and repeated vomiting. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his illness?
options: Rotavirus
Vibrio cholerae
Bacillus cereus
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
approach: Use the time to onset: vomiting within a few hours means a toxin already formed in the food.
Use the food: rice left warm lets spores germinate and make toxin.
Match reheated rice to Bacillus cereus.
questions.why: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking. When cooked rice sits at room temperature, the spores germinate and the bacteria make a heat-stable emetic toxin. Reheating does not destroy this toxin, so vomiting begins within about 1 to 6 hours of eating. A separate diarrheal form appears later, after about 8 to 16 hours.
whyNot: Rotavirus causes watery diarrhea in unvaccinated infants and young children after an incubation of about 2 days.
Vibrio cholerae causes profuse rice-water stools after drinking contaminated water, with an incubation of about 1 to 3 days.
Correct.
Enterotoxigenic E. coli is the classic cause of traveler's diarrhea, with watery stools 1 to 3 days after eating contaminated food or water.

questions.stem: The outbreak continued despite wide use of alcohol-based hand sanitizer. Which of the following best describes the causative virus?
options: Nonenveloped single-stranded RNA calicivirus
Segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus
Enveloped single-stranded RNA coronavirus
Nonenveloped double-stranded DNA enteric adenovirus
approach: Classify norovirus: a calicivirus with a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome.
Recall that it lacks an envelope.
Link the missing envelope to resistance to alcohol and survival on surfaces.
questions.why: Norovirus is a nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus in the calicivirus family. Without a lipid envelope, it resists alcohol-based hand sanitizers, survives on surfaces, and tolerates freezing and mild heat. A very small dose causes infection, and patients shed large amounts in vomit and stool. These traits make it the leading cause of outbreaks on cruise ships and in nursing homes, schools, and restaurants, where soap and water and bleach-based cleaning are needed.
whyNot: Correct.
Rotavirus is a segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus. It mainly affects unvaccinated infants and young children.
Enveloped viruses are inactivated readily by alcohol. Coronaviruses are mainly respiratory pathogens.
Enteric adenovirus types 40 and 41 cause diarrhea mostly in young children, not adult outbreaks.

questions.stem: She is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium chloride. Which of the following best explains why adding glucose increases intestinal water absorption?
options: Glucose enters by GLUT5 and pulls water in by osmosis
SGLT1 couples sodium uptake to glucose at the brush border
Glucose closes CFTR chloride channels in crypt cells
Glucose raises insulin, which adds aquaporins to enterocytes
approach: Recall how glucose crosses the apical membrane: SGLT1, with two sodium ions per glucose.
Note that SGLT1 keeps working during most infectious diarrheas.
Link solute absorption to water following it across the epithelium.
questions.why: SGLT1 on the brush border carries two sodium ions with each glucose or galactose molecule into the enterocyte. Glucose leaves the cell through GLUT2 on the basolateral side, and sodium is pumped out by Na+/K+-ATPase. The absorbed solute creates an osmotic gradient, and water follows. This transporter remains largely functional in most acute diarrheal illnesses, so a solution with both glucose and sodium restores fluid even while diarrhea continues.
whyNot: GLUT5 transports fructose by facilitated diffusion, without sodium. Glucose enters by SGLT1.
Correct.
Glucose does not close CFTR. Cholera toxin opens CFTR by raising cAMP.
Insulin does not control water uptake in the intestine, and enterocyte glucose uptake does not depend on insulin.

questions.stem: Her symptoms persist for 3 weeks, and she undergoes upper endoscopy with biopsy of the proximal small intestine. Which of the following features identifies the specimen as duodenum rather than jejunum?
options: Peyer patches in the mucosa and submucosa
Goblet cells scattered among absorptive cells
Villi lined by simple columnar epithelium
Mucous glands in the submucosa
approach: List what all small bowel segments share: villi, simple columnar epithelium, and goblet cells.
Find the feature unique to the duodenum.
Link Brunner glands to their alkaline mucus, which protects against acid from the stomach.
questions.why: Brunner glands are coiled mucous glands in the submucosa of the duodenum. They secrete alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus that helps neutralize acid from the stomach and protects the duodenal mucosa. The jejunum lacks these glands and has tall, closely spaced plicae circulares, and the ileum has Peyer patches.
whyNot: Peyer patches identify the ileum.
Goblet cells occur throughout the small intestine and colon, so they do not identify a segment.
Villi with simple columnar epithelium line the whole small intestine.
Correct.

dx: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis in a toddler
case: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of 3 days of fever, irritability, drooling, and refusal to eat or drink. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows swollen, erythematous gingiva that bleed easily, clusters of small vesicles and shallow ulcers on the gingiva, anterior tongue, and lips, and tender submandibular and anterior cervical lymph nodes. Mucous membranes are dry. A Tzanck smear of a vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells, and PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). Diagnosis: primary herpetic gingivostomatitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient most reliably distinguishes his illness from herpangina?
options: High fever with irritability and refusal to drink
Gingivitis with lip and anterior oral vesicles
Vesicles that progress to shallow ulcers
Occurrence in a child younger than 5 years
approach: Recall herpangina: coxsackie A virus with vesicles on the soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars.
Recall primary HSV-1: inflamed, bleeding gums and vesicles in the front of the mouth and on the lips.
Pick the feature found in only one of the two.
questions.why: Both illnesses strike young children with fever, sore mouth, and vesicles that become ulcers. Primary HSV-1 gingivostomatitis involves the front of the mouth: swollen, bleeding gingiva and vesicles on the gums, tongue, buccal mucosa, and lips. Herpangina, caused by coxsackie A viruses, places vesicles at the back of the mouth on the soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar pillars, and the gums are spared. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackie A16) adds vesicles on the palms and soles.
whyNot: Both illnesses can cause high fever, irritability, and poor intake.
Correct.
Vesicles become ulcers in both illnesses.
Both occur mostly in young children.

questions.stem: After the illness resolves, the virus remains latent and can later reactivate as cold sores. Latent virus that infected the anterior tongue and lower gingiva most likely resides in neurons of which of the following ganglia?
options: Geniculate ganglion
Inferior ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve
Submandibular ganglion
Trigeminal ganglion
approach: Recall that HSV travels up sensory axons and stays latent in their cell bodies.
Map general sensation: anterior two thirds of the tongue by the lingual nerve and lower gingiva by branches of V3.
Find the ganglion that holds these sensory cell bodies.
questions.why: HSV-1 enters the endings of sensory neurons in the mucosa and travels by retrograde axonal transport to their cell bodies, where it stays latent. General sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue travels in the lingual nerve, and the lower gums are supplied by other branches of the mandibular nerve (V3). The cell bodies of these neurons lie in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation sends virus back down the axons, usually causing cold sores on the lip.
whyNot: The geniculate ganglion holds the cell bodies of chorda tympani taste fibers (facial nerve). The gingiva has no taste fibers, so general sensory neurons are the better fit.
The inferior glossopharyngeal ganglion holds sensory neurons for the posterior third of the tongue and the pharynx.
The submandibular ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands, with no sensory cell bodies.
Correct.

topics: Sensory innervation of the tongue and gums

questions.stem: Because of his painful mouth and fever, he drinks little, and his salivary flow falls. If salivary flow stayed low for months, loss of which of the following salivary functions would most directly promote dental caries?
options: Starch digestion by salivary amylase
Fat digestion by lingual lipase
Bicarbonate buffering of plaque acid
Lubrication of food by mucins
approach: Recall that caries forms when plaque bacteria make acid that dissolves enamel.
Ask which salivary function opposes this acid.
Pick bicarbonate buffering, which also allows calcium and phosphate to remineralize enamel.
questions.why: Dental caries forms when bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans ferment sugars into acid that dissolves enamel. Saliva protects teeth in several ways: bicarbonate buffers plaque acid, calcium and phosphate remineralize early lesions, flow washes away sugars, and IgA, lysozyme, and lactoferrin limit bacteria. When flow stays low, as in Sjogren syndrome, after head and neck radiation, or with anticholinergic drugs, caries develops rapidly, often at the gum line.
whyNot: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth, but losing it does not promote caries, and pancreatic amylase completes starch digestion.
Lingual lipase begins fat digestion, mainly in infants, and has no role in protecting enamel.
Correct.
Mucins lubricate food for swallowing, and their loss makes chewing and swallowing harder, but buffering of acid is the key defense against caries.

questions.stem: Secretory IgA in his saliva helps neutralize viruses on the oral mucosa. Which of the following steps delivers this antibody into saliva in a protease-resistant form?
options: Transcytosis by the polymeric Ig receptor
Leakage of monomeric serum IgA across tight junctions
Transport by the neonatal Fc receptor on acinar cells
Synthesis of IgA by the salivary acinar cells
approach: Recall that plasma cells beneath the epithelium make dimeric IgA joined by a J chain.
Identify the receptor that binds this dimer on the basolateral surface and carries it across the cell.
Note that cleavage at the apical surface leaves a piece of the receptor attached that shields IgA from proteases.
questions.why: Plasma cells in the gland interstitium secrete dimeric IgA linked by a J chain. The polymeric Ig receptor on the basolateral surface of epithelial cells binds the dimer and carries it across the cell by transcytosis. At the apical surface the receptor is cleaved, and a part of it, the secretory component, stays bound to the IgA. Secretory component protects the antibody from proteases in saliva and the gut lumen. Selective IgA deficiency removes this barrier and predisposes to recurrent sinus, lung, and gut infections.
whyNot: Correct.
Serum IgA is mostly monomeric and does not cross intact epithelium in meaningful amounts. Without secretory component it would be degraded.
The neonatal Fc receptor transports IgG across the placenta and protects IgG from breakdown. It does not carry IgA into secretions.
IgA is made by plasma cells, not by epithelial acinar cells. The epithelium only transports it.

topics: Secretory IgA and the polymeric Ig receptor
